title: Building the mix: allocation, diversification, liquidity, emergency fund
objectives: Explain asset allocation and true diversification, not just owning many funds.
Say what liquidity means and why an emergency fund stays out of equity.
body_md:
Asset allocation is how money is split between equity, debt, gold and cash — for example 60% equity, 30% debt, 10% gold. Diversification spreads money across assets, sectors and styles so one fall doesn't sink the whole portfolio; it is not the same as owning many funds that hold the same stocks. Liquidity is how quickly money can be got back without big loss. An emergency fund — usually 6 months of expenses — is kept in savings or liquid funds, not equity.

| Term | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asset allocation | How money is split between equity, debt, gold and cash | 60% equity, 30% debt, 10% gold |
| Diversification | Spreading money across assets, sectors and styles so one fall doesn't sink the whole portfolio | Not the same as owning many funds that hold the same stocks |
| Liquidity | How quickly you can get your money back without big loss | Liquid fund: usually next business day |
| Emergency fund | Money set aside, usually 6 months of expenses, for unexpected needs | Kept in savings or liquid funds, not equity |

> **Investor takeaway:** The right fund is the one whose worst year you could sit through without selling.
example: Five large-cap funds holding the same stocks add little diversification; check portfolio overlap before adding another fund.
say: Five funds holding the same stocks is not diversification.
Emergency money stays in savings or a liquid fund, not equity.
never: Owning many funds always means you are diversified.
An emergency fund should be invested in equity for growth.
